solution.concept_anchor: 52nd Amendment inserting 10th Schedule
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because the 42nd Amendment is a landmark amendment students associate with major structural changes, making it a plausible-sounding wrong answer.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The 42nd Amendment (1976) dealt with fundamental duties, directive principles, and emergency provisions — not the 10th Schedule.
Eliminate option (c): The 61st Amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 — unrelated to defection.
Eliminate option (d): The 73rd Amendment established Panchayati Raj institutions — a different domain entirely.
Confirm option (b): The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 inserted the 10th Schedule alongside amendments to Articles 101, 102, 190, and 191.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students frequently associate landmark constitutional changes with high-profile amendments like the 42nd (1976) or the 44th (1978). The 52nd Amendment is less prominently recalled, making it easy to confuse with neighbouring amendments. A partially prepared student may recall that a major anti-defection reform happened 'around the Emergency period' and incorrectly select the 42nd Amendment.
solution.final_explanation:
The 10th Schedule was not part of the original Constitution — it was inserted through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985, in response to the rampant floor-crossing that had destabilised several state governments during the 1960s and 1970s.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) and made other sweeping changes during the Emergency — it did not introduce the 10th Schedule.
• Option (b) — Correct: The 52nd Amendment Act, 1985 inserted the 10th Schedule and simultaneously amended Articles 101, 102 (parliamentary membership) and 190, 191 (state legislature membership).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The 61st Amendment (1989) lowered the voting age to 18 years.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The 73rd Amendment (1992) gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions.

Value Addition:
• The 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' phenomenon — originating from Haryana MLA Gaya Lal's three-party switches in a single day in 1967 — gave the political impetus for this law.
• The 10th Schedule applies to both Parliament and all state legislatures including Legislative Councils.
• The 52nd Amendment also amended Articles 101(3)(b) and 190(3)(b) to incorporate the disqualification mechanism.

solution.concept_anchor: Paragraph 2 grounds for disqualification

statement_analysis.statement: A member of Parliament is disqualified if they vote contrary to the direction of their political party, even if they had obtained prior permission from the party leadership.
statement_analysis.reason: Paragraph 2(1)(b) explicitly protects a member from disqualification if they have obtained prior permission from the party authority before voting or abstaining contrary to party direction.

statement_analysis.statement: A nominated member of the Rajya Sabha who joins a political party within four months of taking their seat does not incur disqualification under the 10th Schedule.
statement_analysis.reason: Nominated members are given a six-month window to join a political party; joining within six months of taking their seat does not attract disqualification.

statement_analysis.statement: An elected member returned as an independent candidate is disqualified if they join any political party after the declaration of the election result.
statement_analysis.reason: Paragraph 2(2) provides that an independent member (elected without party affiliation) incurs disqualification the moment they join any political party after election.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) appears correct because students who recall Statement 2 correctly may confuse the four-month period with the actual six-month window and dismiss Statement 2 as incorrect, settling for option (c) which excludes it.
elimination_logic: Eliminate Statement 1: The clause 'even if they had obtained prior permission' makes this false — prior permission is a valid exemption under Paragraph 2(1)(b).
Verify Statement 2: The six-month window for nominated members is correct; four months falls within six months, so joining within four months does not disqualify — Statement 2 is correct.
Verify Statement 3: Independent members may not join any party post-election without disqualification — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct; the answer is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 1 is the phrase 'even if they had obtained prior permission' — this is a scope-extension device. Students who know that voting against the party attracts disqualification may miss the exemption clause for prior permission. Statement 2 uses 'four months' (which is within the six-month window) to test whether students know the exact threshold.
solution.final_explanation:
The 10th Schedule's disqualification grounds in Paragraph 2 contain important nuances that are frequently tested.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Paragraph 2(1)(b) disqualifies a member who votes contrary to party direction without prior permission. If prior permission was obtained, no disqualification arises. The statement's qualifier 'even if they had obtained prior permission' inverts the rule.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Nominated members have a six-month window from the date of taking their seat to join a political party. Four months is within this window, so no disqualification occurs.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Under Paragraph 2(2), an elected independent member is disqualified if they join any political party after the election — there is no grace period for them (unlike nominated members).

Value Addition:
• 'Voluntarily giving up membership' under Paragraph 2(1)(a) is broader than formal resignation — even conduct implying severance of party ties can constitute it (Ravi Naik v. Union of India).
• The six-month window is exclusive to nominated members — this distinction between nominated and elected independent members is a classic UPSC trap.
• Even abstaining from a vote, not just voting against, can attract disqualification under Paragraph 2(1)(b).

solution.concept_anchor: Merger provision vs deleted split exemption

statement_analysis.statement: Under the current provisions of the 10th Schedule, a group of legislators can claim exemption from disqualification if at least one-third of the members of the legislature party support a split.
statement_analysis.reason: The one-third 'split' exemption under Paragraph 3 was deleted by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003. No split exemption exists in current law.

statement_analysis.statement: A merger under Paragraph 4 of the 10th Schedule requires that at least two-thirds of the members of the legislature party agree to merge with another political party.
statement_analysis.reason: Paragraph 4 clearly prescribes the two-thirds threshold — this provision remains in force and was not affected by the 91st Amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, which deleted the split provision, also inserted a ceiling on the total number of ministers that can be appointed in a state government.
statement_analysis.reason: The 91st Amendment both deleted Paragraph 3 (split exemption) and inserted the provision capping the Council of Ministers at 15% of the strength of the House (applicable to both Parliament and state legislatures).

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is the strong distractor because Statement 2 about the two-thirds merger threshold sounds similar to the deleted one-third rule, and students may second-guess themselves and mark Statement 2 as also incorrect.
elimination_logic: Identify Statement 1 as incorrect: The one-third split rule under Paragraph 3 was deleted by the 91st Amendment — it no longer exists.
Verify Statement 2 as correct: The two-thirds merger threshold under Paragraph 4 is current law — not incorrect.
Verify Statement 3 as correct: The 91st Amendment simultaneously deleted the split exemption and capped ministerial strength at 15% — this is accurate.
Only Statement 1 is incorrect; the answer is option (c) — 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the common confusion between the deleted one-third split rule (Paragraph 3) and the surviving two-thirds merger rule (Paragraph 4). Students who vaguely recall 'one-third and two-thirds thresholds' may believe both still exist, causing them to mark Statement 2 as also incorrect. The 91st Amendment's dual effect — deleting the split rule AND capping ministerial size — is a frequently overlooked detail.
solution.final_explanation:
The 10th Schedule's exemption framework underwent a critical change in 2003 that UPSC frequently tests.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The one-third split exemption (Paragraph 3) was completely deleted by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003. It is no longer part of the law. Any claim that a one-third split still provides protection is factually wrong.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Paragraph 4 (merger) remains in force. A merger requires a minimum of two-thirds of the legislature party members to agree to merge with another political party — not just any grouping.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 91st Amendment had a dual purpose — it abolished the split exemption AND capped the size of the Council of Ministers at 15% of the total membership of the House (minimum five ministers regardless).

Value Addition:
• The split provision was deleted because it was routinely misused — factions would engineer artificial 'splits' to evade disqualification.
• The 15% cap applies to both the Union Council of Ministers and state Councils of Ministers.
• Under Paragraph 4, the merger must be with another political party — legislators cannot simply form a new independent group and claim merger protection.

solution.concept_anchor: Speaker as adjudicating authority — correct entities

statement_analysis.statement: The President of India decides disqualification petitions under the 10th Schedule for members of the Rajya Sabha.
statement_analysis.reason: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha — not the President — is the adjudicating authority for disqualification petitions involving Rajya Sabha members.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker's decision on a disqualification petition is subject to judicial review by the High Court and the Supreme Court after the final order is passed.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan (1992) held that the Speaker's decision is not final and is subject to judicial review, though courts cannot intervene at the interlocutory stage.

statement_analysis.statement: For members of a state Legislative Council, the Chairman of that Council is the deciding authority for disqualification under the 10th Schedule.
statement_analysis.reason: Paragraph 6 of the 10th Schedule designates the Chairman of a Legislative Council as the deciding authority for its members — mirroring the arrangement for upper houses.

statement_analysis.statement: The Election Commission of India has concurrent jurisdiction with the Speaker to decide anti-defection cases.
statement_analysis.reason: The Election Commission has no jurisdiction under the 10th Schedule for individual disqualification cases — its role is limited to recognising the 'real' political party under the Election Symbols Order, 1968.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) suggests only two statements are correct, which could lure students who wrongly accept the President's role (Statement 1) as partially valid given the President's general constitutional functions.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The President does not decide anti-defection cases — this is the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha's role. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Kihoto Hollohan confirmed judicial review after the final order — Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: The Chairman of a Legislative Council is the designated authority for its members — Statement 3 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 4: The Election Commission has no jurisdiction under the 10th Schedule for individual disqualification — Statement 4 is incorrect.
Only two statements (2 and 3) are correct — the answer is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The strongest trap is Statement 1, which substitutes 'President' for 'Chairman of Rajya Sabha.' Students who know the President's role in electoral disqualifications under Article 103 (consulting the Election Commission) may carry that knowledge over incorrectly into the 10th Schedule context. Statement 4 exploits the real-life overlap between the Election Commission's party recognition role and the Speaker's disqualification role.
solution.final_explanation:
Paragraph 6 of the 10th Schedule is precise about adjudicating authorities, and the UPSC frequently inserts wrong entities into this framework.

Consider the following statements about adjudicating authorities and judicial oversight under the 10th Schedule:

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| President decides Rajya Sabha cases | Incorrect — it is the Chairman of Rajya Sabha |
| Speaker's decision reviewable post-final order | Correct — Kihoto Hollohan, 1992 |
| Chairman of Legislative Council decides for its members | Correct — Paragraph 6 |
| Election Commission has concurrent jurisdiction | Incorrect — no 10th Schedule role |

Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct.

Value Addition:
• In Kihoto Hollohan, the finality clause (Paragraph 6(2)) was struck down by a 5:3 majority as violating the basic structure.
• Courts intervene only after the Speaker's final order — not during pendency of the petition.
• For disqualification of members under Article 103 (Parliament), the President decides after obtaining the Election Commission's opinion — this is a separate mechanism entirely from the 10th Schedule.

solution.concept_anchor: Kihoto Hollohan holdings and 10th Schedule provisions
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) correctly pairs A and D but reverses B and C, which is the most plausible wrong combination for students who recall the Kihoto Hollohan outcome partially.
elimination_logic: Match A-3: The constitutional validity of the 10th Schedule was challenged and upheld in Kihoto Hollohan — not any other case.
Match B-4: Paragraph 6(2) declared the Speaker's decision final and beyond court jurisdiction — this is the finality clause that was struck down.
Match C-1: The Supreme Court held judicial review is permissible only after the Speaker passes the final order — not at the interlocutory stage.
Match D-2: Nemo judex in causa sua (no one a judge in their own cause) was the rationale in Nabam Rebia for limiting the Speaker's power — confirm A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2 → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students familiar with Kihoto Hollohan may conflate the 'finality clause' with the general 'validity of the Schedule' — these are two distinct holdings in the same case. The Nabam Rebia maxim is a Latin legal principle that sounds generic, making it easy to pair with the wrong event. Option (c) is designed to trap students who correctly recall A and D but confuse the finality clause with the interlocutory restriction.
solution.final_explanation:
The Kihoto Hollohan case (1992) contains multiple distinct holdings that must be mapped accurately.

**Correct matches: A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2 → Option (b)**

• A (Constitutional validity of 10th Schedule) → 3 (Upheld in Kihoto Hollohan by the Supreme Court on grounds that it is a reasonable restriction on legislators' freedom)
• B (Paragraph 6(2) of the 10th Schedule) → 4 (Declared the Speaker's decision 'final and not subject to any court's jurisdiction' — this clause was struck down as unconstitutional)
• C (Judicial review of Speaker's decision) → 1 (Permissible only after the final order is passed, not at the interlocutory stage — courts cannot preempt the Speaker's decision mid-proceedings)
• D (Nemo judex in causa sua) → 2 (The Latin maxim applied in Nabam Rebia 2016 — Speaker cannot adjudicate when a removal notice against them is pending)

Value Addition:
• Kihoto Hollohan was decided by a 5:3 majority on the finality clause — it was not unanimous.
• The 'basic structure' doctrine was invoked to strike down the finality clause — judicial review is a basic structure element.
• Nabam Rebia (2016) involved the Arunachal Pradesh political crisis and is a key precedent limiting Speaker's power.

Nabam Rebia vs Deputy Speaker (2016) — Speaker's Power During No-Confidence Motion

solution.concept_anchor: Nabam Rebia — Speaker cannot act when removal notice pending
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) traps students who correctly verify both A and R as factually true but do not pause to test whether R actually causes A — they assume any true R must explain A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. In Nabam Rebia (2016), the Supreme Court held that the Speaker cannot proceed with disqualification petitions when a notice for their own removal is pending.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Paragraph 6 of the 10th Schedule does designate the Speaker as the sole adjudicating authority — this is a true factual claim.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The Nabam Rebia ruling was not premised on Paragraph 6 designating the Speaker — it was premised on the constitutional principle of natural justice (nemo judex in causa sua). R describes a general structural feature, not the reason why the Speaker's power was curtailed in that specific context.
A is correct, R is correct, but R does NOT explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both A and R are individually true statements, making this a classic option (b) trap. Students who verify each statement independently as 'correct' default to option (a) — they skip the causal test. The actual rationale in Nabam Rebia was natural justice (nemo judex), not the structural designation in Paragraph 6. R describes what the Schedule says; A describes a limitation imposed by the Court precisely because that structure creates a conflict of interest.
solution.final_explanation:
The Nabam Rebia case (2016) arose from the Arunachal Pradesh political crisis and is a landmark in the law of anti-defection.

Assertion (A): Factually correct. The Supreme Court held in Nabam Rebia vs Deputy Speaker that a Speaker facing a pending notice of motion for removal cannot proceed to decide disqualification petitions — doing so would amount to the Speaker being a judge in their own cause.

Reason (R): Also factually correct. Paragraph 6 of the 10th Schedule does designate the Speaker/Chairman as the 'sole adjudicating authority' for disqualification questions.

Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. Paragraph 6's designation of the Speaker as the authority is what creates the structural problem — it is the premise for the conflict of interest, not the reason the Court intervened. The Court intervened on the basis of the constitutional principle of natural justice (nemo judex in causa sua), which overrides Paragraph 6's structural designation in situations of personal interest. R explains the Speaker's general power; A describes a judicially imposed limitation on that power arising from a separate constitutional principle.

Correct option: (b)

Value Addition:
• Nabam Rebia has since been referred to a larger Constitution Bench for reconsideration due to concerns about judicial encroachment into legislative affairs.
• The 10th Schedule is completely silent on the question of who decides when the Speaker is the accused — this is a major structural gap.
• The principle nemo judex in causa sua is a foundational principle of natural justice applicable across constitutional adjudication.

solution.concept_anchor: Chronological sequence of anti-defection law amendments
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) places the Dinesh Goswami Committee before the 10th Schedule's insertion, which sounds plausible since committee recommendations often precede legislation — students may assume the committee's work prompted the 1985 law.
elimination_logic: Anchor event: The 10th Schedule was inserted by the 52nd Amendment in 1985 — this must come first among legislative events.
Eliminate option (a): Placing the 91st Amendment before the Kihoto Hollohan judgment is wrong — the case was decided in 1992, and the 91st Amendment came in 2003.
Eliminate option (c): The Dinesh Goswami Committee reported in 1990 — after the 10th Schedule was inserted in 1985, not before.
Eliminate option (d): The Nabam Rebia judgment (2016) cannot precede the 91st Amendment (2003) — that sequence is inverted.

Correct order — 52nd Amendment (1985) → Kihoto Hollohan (1992) → Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990 report, but reform proposals post-1985) → 91st Amendment (2003) → Nabam Rebia (2016) → confirm option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) is the chronological trap — it was set up after the 10th Schedule was in force (1985) to review its working. Students may assume committees precede legislation and place it before 1985. Additionally, the Kihoto Hollohan case (1992) must come before the 91st Amendment (2003) — options that invert this sequence target students who conflate the two reform events.
solution.final_explanation:
The anti-defection law has a specific legislative and judicial chronology that UPSC tests through sequencing questions.

Correct sequence: 52nd Constitutional Amendment (1985) → Kihoto Hollohan judgment (1992) → 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003) → Nabam Rebia judgment (2016)

• 52nd Amendment, 1985: Inserted the 10th Schedule — the foundational event.
• Kihoto Hollohan, 1992: Upheld the Schedule's validity but struck down the finality clause; confirmed judicial review after final order.
• 91st Amendment, 2003: Deleted Paragraph 3 (one-third split exemption) and capped ministerial strength at 15%.
• Nabam Rebia, 2016: Held that the Speaker cannot decide disqualification when a removal notice is pending against them.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (a) reverses Kihoto Hollohan and the 91st Amendment.
• Option (c) places the Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) before the 52nd Amendment (1985) — incorrect; the committee reviewed a law already in force.
• Option (d) inverts the 91st Amendment and Nabam Rebia.

Value Addition:
• The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) was set up specifically to review the working of the 10th Schedule.
• The Law Commission's 170th Report (1999) recommended shifting decision-making to the Election Commission or President.
• Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary (2023) is the most recent landmark — arising from the Maharashtra political crisis.

solution.concept_anchor: No statutory time limit for Speaker — judicially imposed timeline
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because 'three months' is a real timeline mentioned in specific Supreme Court orders, leading students to believe this is a constitutional requirement rather than a judicially imposed case-specific direction.
elimination_logic: Identify the core question: Is there a constitutionally or legislatively mandated time limit for the Speaker to decide a disqualification petition?
Eliminate option (a): The Constitution prescribes no 30-day limit for anti-defection petitions — this is a fabricated provision.

Eliminate option (b): While courts have in specific cases directed Speakers to decide within three months, this is a judicially imposed case-specific direction, not a constitutional or statutory mandate.
Eliminate option (c): No six-month deadline exists anywhere in the 10th Schedule or related constitutional provisions.
Confirm option (d): The 10th Schedule is silent on any time limit — the Speaker may take as long as the term of the House, which is the structural lacuna courts have repeatedly noted.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 'three months' in option (b) is a real number that appears in specific Supreme Court orders directing Speakers to decide petitions expeditiously. Students who have encountered this figure may treat it as a statutory requirement. The trap is that a judicially imposed, case-specific direction is not the same as a constitutionally prescribed limit — and the 10th Schedule itself contains no time limit whatsoever.
solution.final_explanation:
A disqualification petition is filed against a sitting member of a state legislature in June. The Speaker does not set a hearing date for several months. The petitioners approach the High Court seeking a direction to the Speaker to decide the petition within a fixed time. The High Court wants to know what the constitutional position is regarding the time limit for the Speaker's decision.

The applicable principle: The 10th Schedule prescribes no specific time limit within which the Speaker must decide a disqualification petition. This is a well-documented structural lacuna — Speakers have exploited it by deferring decisions until the term of the legislature expires, effectively nullifying the petition.

• Option (a): A 30-day constitutional limit does not exist in the 10th Schedule or anywhere in the Constitution — this is a fabricated provision.
• Option (b): Three months is not a statutory mandate; it has appeared only in specific Supreme Court orders as a case-by-case judicial direction — not a universal constitutional rule.
• Option (c): No six-month deadline is prescribed anywhere in the 10th Schedule.
• Option (d): Correct — the Schedule is completely silent on time limits. The High Court can note this lacuna and may direct the Speaker to decide within a reasonable time, but this arises from judicial discretion, not constitutional prescription.

Value Addition:
• The Manipur and Goa cases are frequently cited as examples of deliberate delay by Speakers in deciding disqualification petitions.
• The Law Commission (170th Report) and several constitutional experts have recommended a fixed statutory timeline.
• In Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020), the Supreme Court directed the Manipur Speaker to decide a petition within four weeks — illustrating the judicial power to impose timelines without a statutory basis.

solution.concept_anchor: Consequences of anti-defection disqualification vs RPA disqualification
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) about being barred from ministerial appointment sounds like an additional punishment and students may suspect it is the fabricated option — but it is actually a real consequence (read with Articles 75 and 164).
elimination_logic: Identify the category: all options describe consequences — the odd one is a consequence that does NOT actually flow from anti-defection disqualification.
Confirm option (a): Loss of seat is the primary consequence of disqualification — confirmed.
Confirm option (b): A disqualified member cannot be appointed Minister until re-elected — confirmed under Articles 75 and 164 read with the disqualification.

Test option (c): A bar on contesting elections for a fixed period is NOT a consequence of 10th Schedule disqualification — this applies under the Representation of the People Act, 1951 for specific offences, not under anti-defection law.
Confirm option (d): The member ceases to be part of the House and all associated privileges — confirmed.
Option (c) is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students conflate anti-defection disqualification with the electoral disqualification provisions under the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The RPA does bar convicted persons from contesting elections for fixed periods, but no such bar applies upon 10th Schedule disqualification — the member can immediately contest a by-election from the same or any other constituency. This is a direct consequence of the two systems operating independently.
solution.final_explanation:
The consequences of disqualification under the 10th Schedule are specific and must not be confused with consequences under the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

• Option (a) — Common consequence: The disqualified member loses their seat immediately — they cease to be a member of Parliament or the state legislature.
• Option (b) — Common consequence: Since the member is no longer a legislator, they cannot hold a ministerial post until re-elected (Articles 75(5) and 164(4) require ministers to be members of the legislature within six months).
• Option (c) — NOT a consequence of 10th Schedule disqualification: A bar on contesting elections for a fixed period is imposed under the RPA, 1951 for specific disqualifications (e.g., conviction for electoral offences) — it is not a consequence of anti-defection disqualification. The member can contest a by-election immediately.
• Option (d) — Common consequence: Loss of membership entails cessation of all parliamentary privileges, salary, and participation rights.

Value Addition:
• This distinction — that anti-defection disqualification does not bar future candidacy — is a frequently tested UPSC fact.
• A disqualified member can even rejoin the same party and contest from the same seat.
• Electoral disqualification under the RPA (e.g., for corrupt practices) is far more severe and can extend up to six years.

solution.concept_anchor: Political party vs legislature party — distinct jurisdictions

statement_analysis.statement: A split among elected members within a legislature party constitutes a 'merger' under Paragraph 4 of the 10th Schedule, provided two-thirds of the legislature party agrees.
statement_analysis.reason: Paragraph 4 requires a merger at the level of the 'political party' — not merely a regrouping within the legislature party. A split among legislators forming a separate bloc within the House does not qualify as a merger unless the political party itself merges with another party.

statement_analysis.statement: The Election Commission of India determines which faction represents the 'real' political party using the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, a process separate from the Speaker's jurisdiction under the 10th Schedule.
statement_analysis.reason: The Election Commission's jurisdiction under the Symbols Order, 1968 is distinct from the Speaker's jurisdiction under the 10th Schedule — both processes can run in parallel and may produce different outcomes regarding the same political group.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is the strong distractor because students who recall that a two-thirds majority can protect from disqualification may assume Statement 1 is correct, confusing legislature party rearrangements with the merger requirement.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The merger under Paragraph 4 must be between political parties — not just an intra-House regrouping. Statement 1 incorrectly equates a legislature-level split with a merger. Statement 1 is incorrect.

Evaluate Statement 2: The Election Commission uses the Symbols Order, 1968 independently of the Speaker's 10th Schedule authority — these are parallel processes with different outcomes possible. Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the common conflation of 'legislature party' and 'political party.' The two-thirds rule for merger applies when the political party merges with another party — a faction within the legislature deciding to act together does not constitute a merger under Paragraph 4. The Maharashtra crisis (Shiv Sena, 2023) exposed this distinction sharply. Statement 2 is often under-appreciated as a separate parallel process.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between 'political party' and 'legislature party' is one of the most nuanced and frequently tested aspects of the 10th Schedule.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Paragraph 4's merger provision operates at the level of the political party — the organisation outside the legislature. If a group of legislators simply decides to act as a separate unit within the House (even with two-thirds support), that does not constitute a 'merger' under the Schedule. The merger must involve the parent political party merging with another registered party. The Shiv Sena (2023) case clarified this definitively.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Election Commission exercises a wholly separate jurisdiction under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968. It determines which faction of a split party is the 'real' party entitled to the original party name and symbol. This process runs in parallel with the Speaker's disqualification proceedings and can yield outcomes that are in tension with each other.

Value Addition:
• In the Shiv Sena crisis, both processes ran simultaneously — the Supreme Court adjudicated on the Speaker's powers while the Election Commission separately awarded the party symbol.
• The Symbols Order, 1968 uses 'majority support among elected members' as one test — this can create a situation where the larger legislative faction gets the symbol but its members are still disqualified by the Speaker.
• This dual-track system is widely regarded as an institutional design flaw requiring legislative resolution.

solution.concept_anchor: Dinesh Goswami Committee recommendation on anti-defection
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because the Law Commission (170th Report) did recommend transferring decision-making to the Election Commission — students may attribute this recommendation to the Goswami Committee.
elimination_logic: Identify the committee: The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) specifically reviewed the anti-defection law.
Eliminate option (a): The Goswami Committee did not recommend abolishing the anti-defection law entirely.
Eliminate option (c): Transferring power to the Election Commission was the Law Commission's recommendation (170th Report, 1999) — not Goswami's.
Eliminate option (d): Extending disqualification to Rajya Sabha only was not any committee's recommendation.
Confirm option (b): The Goswami Committee recommended limiting disqualification to cases of voting against no-confidence motions and money bills — the narrowest form of the law.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) is particularly dangerous because the Law Commission did recommend exactly what it states — transferring decision-making to the Election Commission. Students who remember this recommendation but attribute it to the wrong committee will select option (c) confidently. The Goswami Committee's narrower recommendation (only no-confidence motions and money bills) is the correct attribution.
solution.final_explanation:
The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) was set up to examine the working of the anti-defection law after it had been in operation for five years.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: No major committee recommended abolishing the anti-defection law entirely — the consensus was on narrowing its scope.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Goswami Committee recommended restricting disqualification to only two situations — when a member votes against a motion of no-confidence and when a member votes against a money bill. This would preserve legislative freedom in routine voting while protecting government stability.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: This recommendation (transferring the power to decide from the Speaker to the Election Commission or the President/Governor) was made by the Law Commission in its 170th Report (1999) — not by the Goswami Committee.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: No committee recommended restricting the law's application to Rajya Sabha only.

Value Addition:
• The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (2002) had a similar view — disqualification should be limited to votes that threaten the government's survival.
• The Law Commission (255th Report, 2015) reiterated the recommendation to shift adjudicating power to an independent body.
• Currently, no legislative reform has been implemented — the law applies to all votes where a whip is issued.

solution.concept_anchor: Voluntarily giving up membership — Ravi Naik interpretation
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is the strong distractor because it correctly states that abstaining from voting can attract disqualification — this is true — but pairs it with an incorrect claim about the whip, making the pair as a whole wrong.
elimination_logic: Test option (a): 'Voluntarily giving up membership requires submission of a formal resignation letter' — this is wrong. Ravi Naik vs Union of India held that conduct implying severance of party ties is sufficient; formal resignation is not required.

Test option (b): 'Abstaining from voting against party directions can attract disqualification — true. But 'only if the party issues a three-line whip' — this is a fabricated requirement. The law says 'direction of the political party', not specifically a three-line whip.
Test option (c): 'A nominated member joining a party within six months is disqualified' — this is wrong. Nominated members have six months to join a party without disqualification.

Test option (d): 'The grounds of disqualification apply to both elected and nominated members, but the rules differ' — correct. Paragraph 2(1) applies to elected members and Paragraph 2 also covers nominated members with the specific six-month window. The pair accurately captures differential treatment. Confirm option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) exploits the intuitive assumption that 'giving up membership' must involve a formal act like a resignation letter. The Supreme Court in Ravi Naik expressly rejected this — even conduct that unmistakably signals departure from the party suffices. Option (b) introduces 'three-line whip' — a concept from British parliamentary practice — which has no statutory basis under the Indian 10th Schedule.
solution.final_explanation:
The 10th Schedule's disqualification grounds contain several nuances that are frequently mis-stated.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: 'Voluntarily giving up membership' under Paragraph 2(1)(a) does not require a formal resignation letter. The Supreme Court in Ravi Naik vs Union of India (1994) held that conduct — such as supporting an opposing party or making public statements against one's party — can constitute voluntary giving up of membership.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: While abstaining from voting does attract disqualification, there is no requirement of a 'three-line whip' specifically. The test is whether a direction was issued by the 'political party' — the number of lines on the whip notice is a British convention with no Indian constitutional basis.
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: A nominated member who joins a party within six months does NOT incur disqualification — the six months is a permitted window for joining.
• Option (d) — Correctly matched: The 10th Schedule applies to both elected and nominated members, but the rules differ — elected independents cannot join any party post-election, while nominated members have a six-month window to join.

Value Addition:
• Ravi Naik (1994) is one of the foundational judgments on what constitutes 'voluntary giving up' of party membership.
• The 'three-line whip' concept is from Westminster parliamentary practice and has no direct Indian constitutional equivalent.
• This distinction between elected independent members (no joining allowed) and nominated members (six months to join) is a favourite UPSC trap.

solution.concept_anchor: 10th Schedule applicability — all Houses including upper houses

statement_analysis.statement: The 10th Schedule applies to both Houses of Parliament and to all state legislative assemblies, but does not apply to state Legislative Councils.
statement_analysis.reason: The 10th Schedule applies to both Houses of Parliament and all state legislatures — including state Legislative Councils (Vidhan Parishads) wherever they exist.

statement_analysis.statement: For members of the Rajya Sabha, the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha acts as the deciding authority for disqualification under the 10th Schedule.
statement_analysis.reason: Paragraph 6 designates the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha as the deciding authority for disqualification petitions relating to Rajya Sabha members.

statement_analysis.statement: The 10th Schedule applies to members of state Legislative Councils, and the Chairman of the Legislative Council is the designated deciding authority for disqualification in such cases.
statement_analysis.reason: The Schedule's provisions cover all Houses — including state upper houses — and the Chairman of the Legislative Council mirrors the Speaker's role for the lower house.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) includes Statement 1, which sounds plausible because directly elected chambers are more prominently associated with defection in popular discourse.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: This contains 'does not apply to state Legislative Councils' — this is factually wrong. The Schedule applies to all Houses. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha decides disqualification for Rajya Sabha members — correct under Paragraph 6.
Evaluate Statement 3: The Schedule does apply to Legislative Councils and the Chairman of the Legislative Council is the deciding authority — correct.
Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is the scope-extension trap — it restricts the Schedule's application by excluding Legislative Councils, which is a common misconception. Students who associate anti-defection primarily with Lok Sabha and state assemblies (the directly elected houses) may incorrectly accept Statement 1 as true, not realising the Schedule expressly covers all Houses including upper chambers.
solution.final_explanation:
The 10th Schedule's applicability is broad and covers every legislative chamber in India — not only directly elected ones.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Schedule applies to state Legislative Councils as well. The addition of 'does not apply to state Legislative Councils' is factually wrong — this is the scope-extension trap.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Paragraph 6 designates the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha as the deciding authority for disqualification petitions relating to its members — exactly mirroring the Speaker's role in the Lok Sabha.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Schedule covers all Houses of Parliament and all state legislatures (both assemblies and councils). The Chairman of the Legislative Council is the designated deciding authority for its members.

Value Addition:
• The 52nd Amendment simultaneously amended Articles 101 and 102 (parliamentary membership) as well as Articles 190 and 191 (state legislature membership) to bring all Houses within the anti-defection framework.
• Currently six states have Legislative Councils: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Bihar, and Uttar Pradesh.
• Defection cases involving upper house members are rarer but legally treated identically to lower house cases.

solution.concept_anchor: 10th Schedule vs Article 105 — reasonable restriction holding
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The 10th Schedule does restrict how members vote by tying their votes to party directions under pain of disqualification — creating a real tension with Article 105 which guarantees freedom of speech and vote inside Parliament.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan held that the 10th Schedule is a constitutionally valid reasonable restriction and does not violate Article 105.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The Court in Kihoto Hollohan directly addressed the tension identified in A and resolved it by holding that party discipline is a reasonable restriction — R is the judicial resolution of the tension described in A.
Both A and R are correct, and R explains A → correct option is (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The tension between the 10th Schedule and Article 105 is one of the most intellectually rich aspects of the anti-defection law.

Assertion (A): Factually correct. Article 105 guarantees freedom of speech and the right to vote to every member of Parliament — but the 10th Schedule conditions voting behaviour on party directions, imposing disqualification for deviation. This is a genuine constitutional tension.

Reason (R): Also factually correct. In Kihoto Hollohan vs Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court directly addressed this conflict and held that the 10th Schedule imposes a reasonable restriction on members' freedom of vote — one that is justified by the need for party discipline, political stability, and the mandate on which the member was elected. The restriction was found not to violate Article 105.

Causal relationship: R directly explains why the tension described in A does not invalidate the Schedule — the Court's holding in Kihoto Hollohan is the resolution of the very conflict articulated in A. Both are correct and R causally explains A.

Correct option: (a)

Value Addition:
• Critics argue that the law turns legislators into 'rubber stamps,' undermining the deliberative democracy that the Constitution envisions.
• Article 194 is the state legislature equivalent of Article 105 — the same tension exists for state assembly members.
• Countries like the UK allow 'free votes' or 'conscience votes' on certain issues — Indian law has no equivalent exemption.

solution.concept_anchor: Subhash Desai 2023 — Governor's role and Speaker's disqualification powers

statement_analysis.statement: In Subhash Desai vs Principal Secretary (2023), the Supreme Court upheld the Governor's decision to invite the Eknath Shinde faction to form the government, holding that the Governor acted within constitutional bounds.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court in Subhash Desai held that the Governor's invitation to the Shinde faction to form the government was improper given the circumstances — it did not uphold the Governor's action.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court in Subhash Desai (2023) referred the question of the Speaker's disqualification powers during a political crisis to a larger Constitution Bench for comprehensive resolution.
statement_analysis.reason: Recognising the complexity of the intersection between the 10th Schedule, Governor's powers, and the Speaker's position, the Court referred this question to a larger bench rather than deciding it finally.

statement_analysis.statement: The Court in Subhash Desai (2023) held that the anti-defection law does not apply to members of a legislature party who switch allegiance, provided the original political party has itself split.
statement_analysis.reason: No such holding was made in Subhash Desai. The Court did not create any new exemption — it reinforced that a split among legislature party members does not constitute a merger or split at the political party level for 10th Schedule purposes.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) would suggest only Statement 3 is incorrect, which tempts students who vaguely recall that 'the Court did something with the Governor' but are unsure whether it upheld or struck down his action.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: The Court found the Governor's invitation improper — not within constitutional bounds. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Test Statement 2: The Court did refer the larger question to a Constitution Bench — Statement 2 is correct, so it is not the answer.
Test Statement 3: No exemption for political party splits was announced in Subhash Desai — this is a fabricated holding. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the genuine complexity of the Subhash Desai case — students may recall only that 'the Supreme Court decided something about the Governor' without remembering that it found the Governor's action improper. Statement 3 fabricates a new exemption that was never part of the judgment, relying on the plausible logic that a political party split should follow different rules — but the Court explicitly rejected this.
solution.final_explanation:
Subhash Desai vs Principal Secretary (2023) arose from the Maharashtra political crisis involving the Shiv Sena split and is one of the most recent significant judgments on the intersection of anti-defection law, Governor's powers, and the Speaker's constitutional position.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: The Supreme Court did not uphold the Governor's action. It held that the Governor's invitation to the Shinde faction to form government was improper — the Governor did not have sufficient grounds to conclude that the incumbent government had lost majority without a floor test.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Court referred the broader question of the Speaker's disqualification powers during a political crisis to a larger Constitution Bench, recognising that these intersecting issues require a comprehensive constitutional ruling.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: The Court made no such ruling. It did not create any exemption from the 10th Schedule for members whose political party has undergone a split — this is a fabricated holding.

Value Addition:
• The case also reiterated that a newly elected Speaker cannot be appointed from a faction whose members' disqualification is pending — echoing Nabam Rebia's principle.
• The Shiv Sena dispute involved both the 10th Schedule proceedings before the Speaker and the Election Commission's recognition of the 'real' Shiv Sena — both running simultaneously.
• This case is relevant for both anti-defection law and constitutional questions about the Governor's discretionary powers.

solution.concept_anchor: Reform committees and their recommendations on anti-defection
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) correctly pairs A and B but swaps C and D, which is the most likely error for a student who knows Dinesh Goswami and Law Commission but confuses NCRWC's recommendation with the Law Commission's.
elimination_logic: Match A-3: The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) recommended restricting disqualification to no-confidence motions and money bills — this is a well-known specific recommendation.

Match B-1: The Law Commission's 170th Report (1999) recommended transferring the adjudicating power from the Speaker to the Election Commission or President/Governor — distinct from scope restriction.

Match C-4: The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (2002) recommended disqualification only for votes threatening the government's survival — similar to Goswami in spirit but different in specifics.

Match D-2: The 10th Schedule itself contains no time limit for the Speaker — the judicially imposed timelines come from court orders in specific cases, not from the Schedule. Confirm A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap operates between B (Law Commission recommending Election Commission) and C (NCRWC). Students who know one recommendation tend to attribute both to the same body, or confuse which committee said what. The Law Commission's specific recommendation to transfer power to the Election Commission is the key distinguishing fact. D is a factual-negative item — the Schedule's silence on time limits — which requires the student to recall what the Schedule does NOT say.
solution.final_explanation:
The reform discourse around the anti-defection law involves multiple committees whose distinct recommendations must be mapped accurately.

**Correct matches: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → Option (b)**

• A (Dinesh Goswami Committee, 1990) → 3: Recommended limiting disqualification to votes on no-confidence motions and money bills — the narrowest reform proposal.
• B (Law Commission, 170th Report, 1999) → 1: Recommended that the adjudicating power be transferred from the Speaker to the Election Commission or the President/Governor — addressing the conflict of interest at the Speaker's level.
• C (NCRWC, 2002) → 4: Recommended disqualification only for votes that could cause the government to fall — broader than Goswami but still a narrowing of current law.
• D (10th Schedule, Paragraph 6) → 2: The Schedule is completely silent on any time limit for the Speaker's decision — this silence is the structural lacuna courts have tried to fill through specific directions.

Value Addition:
• No legislative reform based on any of these committee recommendations has been implemented as of date.
• The Law Commission reiterated its recommendation in the 255th Report (2015).
• The conflict of interest problem (Speaker deciding on behalf of their own party) remains the central unremedied structural flaw.

solution.concept_anchor: Indian anti-defection law strictness vs conscience vote in other systems
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students who know that India has a strict anti-defection regime may select it under the impression that abstaining requires explicit party permission in all cases.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Indian law does not permit conscience votes — abstaining from a vote against party direction itself attracts disqualification. The UK and USA permit conscience votes, not India.

Eliminate option (c): While prior permission exempts a member, the blanket statement that 'abstaining is permitted if disclosed to the party whip' is not accurate — the member needs permission from the authorised party authority, not merely disclosure.
Eliminate option (d): Indian law does not treat voting and abstaining differently in terms of both being potentially disqualifying — the option creates a false hierarchy.

Confirm option (b): In the UK and USA, legislators may vote according to their conscience on issues where the party permits free votes — Indian law has no such provision and even abstaining against party direction can attract disqualification.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) presents the 'conscience vote' concept but misattributes it to India — students who have read about international comparisons may recall the term but fail to note that it applies to UK/USA, not India. Option (c) introduces the real nuance of prior permission but garbles it into 'mere disclosure to the whip', which is incorrect — permission must come from the authorised party body.
solution.final_explanation:
India's anti-defection law is among the most stringent in the democratic world, particularly in its treatment of voting discipline.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Indian law does not permit conscience votes. It is the UK and USA that allow legislators to vote freely on certain issues. India's 10th Schedule conditions voting on party directions.
• Option (b) — Correct: In the UK and USA, legislators are permitted free or conscience votes on selected issues without facing any legal consequence. India has no such provision — a member who votes or abstains contrary to party direction without prior permission faces disqualification.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The exemption for deviation requires prior permission from the 'authorised body of the political party' — not merely informing the whip. Disclosure alone does not protect the member.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Both voting against and abstaining from voting against party direction can attract disqualification — the Schedule treats both identically.

Value Addition:
• In the UK, 'three-line whips' signal the most serious votes; rebellion is common even on two-line whips without legal consequence.
• India's strictness reflects the instability that floor-crossing caused in the 1960s-70s — the law prioritises government stability over legislative freedom.
• The absence of a conscience vote provision is one of the most cited criticisms of the Indian anti-defection regime by comparative constitutional scholars.

solution.concept_anchor: Paragraph 2(1)(b) — prior permission exemption from disqualification
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because it correctly identifies Paragraph 2(1)(b) as the relevant provision but incorrectly concludes that prior permission given to the whip (not the 'authorised political party body') is sufficient.
elimination_logic: Identify the legal question: Does voting contrary to party direction with prior permission from the authorised party body attract disqualification?
Eliminate option (a): Disqualification is not automatic upon voting against the party — the exemption for prior permission must be evaluated first.

Eliminate option (b): Prior permission to the whip alone may not suffice — the permission must come from the authorised body of the political party. The option also conflates whip with authorised party authority.
Eliminate option (c): No provision in the 10th Schedule creates a general exception for votes on private members' bills.

Confirm option (d): Paragraph 2(1)(b) explicitly carves out an exemption — a member who obtains prior permission from the authorised body of the political party before voting contrary to party direction does not incur disqualification.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario is designed so that 'prior permission' is present — the critical legal fact that triggers the exemption. Option (b) is the key trap: it introduces the correct paragraph number and says 'prior permission' but attributes the permission to the whip rather than the 'authorised political party body.' A student who reads quickly and sees 'Paragraph 2(1)(b)' and 'prior permission' may select option (b) without catching the crucial distinction about who grants the permission.
solution.final_explanation:
A Member of Parliament announces publicly that she intends to vote against her party's official position on a pending bill. Before the vote, she formally applies to and receives written permission from her party's national executive — the authorised party body — to vote as per her constituency's interest. She then votes against the party line.

The applicable principle is Paragraph 2(1)(b) of the 10th Schedule, which disqualifies a member who votes or abstains contrary to party direction unless they have obtained prior permission from the authorised body of the political party.

• Option (a): Incorrect — disqualification is not automatic upon voting against the party. The exemption clause must be applied.
• Option (b): Incorrect — while Paragraph 2(1)(b) is the correct provision, permission from the party whip is not necessarily equivalent to permission from the 'authorised political party body.' Here, the national executive granted permission — a higher authority than the whip, satisfying the exemption fully.
• Option (c): Incorrect — the 10th Schedule draws no general distinction between votes on government bills and private members' bills for disqualification purposes.
• Option (d): Correct — since the member obtained prior permission from the authorised body of her political party, she squarely falls within the exemption carved out by Paragraph 2(1)(b). No disqualification arises.

Value Addition:
• The authorised party body may vary by party constitution — it could be the national executive, parliamentary board, or a designated officer.
• Retroactive condonation (party condoning the vote after the fact) has been recognised in some cases as protecting the member from disqualification.
• The concept of 'authorised body' adds an important evidentiary question to disqualification proceedings — who exactly granted permission and in what capacity.

solution.concept_anchor: 91st Amendment — dual effect: split deletion and ministerial cap

statement_analysis.statement: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 deleted Paragraph 3 of the 10th Schedule, which had earlier permitted a group of legislators forming one-half of the legislature party to break away without attracting disqualification.
statement_analysis.reason: Paragraph 3 permitted a group of one-third (not one-half) of the legislature party to break away without disqualification. The fraction mentioned in the statement is factually wrong.

statement_analysis.statement: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 also capped the size of the Council of Ministers at 15% of the total strength of the lower house of Parliament or the state legislature, as the case may be.
statement_analysis.reason: The 91st Amendment simultaneously introduced this cap as part of addressing the political misuse of large cabinets that were assembled as rewards for defectors, applicable to both Parliament and state legislatures.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is the strong distractor because students may recall 'one-third' and 'one-half' as two different possible thresholds and not be certain which was in Paragraph 3, accepting both statements as correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The original Paragraph 3 required one-third of the legislature party — not one-half — for a valid split. Statement 1 substitutes 'one-half' for 'one-third', making it factually incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: The 15% cap on Council of Ministers was indeed introduced by the 91st Amendment — this is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The fraction in Statement 1 is the precision trap. Students who remember that Paragraph 3 involved a fractional threshold but cannot recall whether it was one-third or one-half are likely to accept Statement 1 as correct. The actual threshold was one-third — making 'one-half' a temporal-swap variant that tests precision of recall.
solution.final_explanation:
The 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003) is notable for two simultaneous changes, both of which are testable.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The original Paragraph 3 of the 10th Schedule (before deletion) required that at least one-third of the members of the legislature party break away to constitute a valid 'split' exemption. The statement incorrectly states 'one-half'. The one-third threshold was itself widely criticised as too easy to engineer, which led to its deletion.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 91st Amendment also inserted the provision capping the Council of Ministers at 15% of the total strength of the lower house (with a minimum of 12 members). This cap was introduced in Articles 75(1A) and 164(1A) simultaneously — it applies to the Union Cabinet and state Cabinets.

Value Addition:
• The political context for deleting Paragraph 3 was that parties engineering defections would carefully orchestrate splits to cross the one-third threshold — making defection legally risk-free for sufficiently large groups.
• The minimum of 12 ministers (regardless of House strength) ensures small states have functional cabinets.
• The 15% cap has reduced the practice of awarding ministerial positions as rewards for floor-crossing support.

solution.concept_anchor: Kihoto Hollohan — majority vote and basic structure
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'unanimous' is the strong distractor because the constitutional validity of the 10th Schedule was upheld — students may assume this was a consensus outcome and select 'unanimous' without knowing the bench was divided.
elimination_logic: Identify the claim: The finality clause in Paragraph 6(2) was struck down — at what majority?
Eliminate option (b): The judgment was not unanimous — it was a divided bench.
Eliminate option (c): A 4:1 majority would imply only one dissent on a five-judge bench — this is not the reported majority for this specific holding.
Eliminate option (d): A 3:2 majority would indicate a near-even split — this is not the reported outcome.

Confirm option (a): Kihoto Hollohan was decided by a five-judge Constitution Bench; the finality clause was struck down by a 5:3 majority — but wait, on a five-judge bench the maximum possible split is 5:0, 4:1, or 3:2. A five-judge bench cannot produce a 5:3 majority. The reported majority for striking down the finality clause was 3:2. Re-evaluate: correct option is (d) — 3:2 majority.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Kihoto Hollohan bench was a Constitution Bench of five judges. The finality clause (Paragraph 6(2)) was struck down by a majority of 3:2. Students who recall 'the Schedule was upheld' may conflate the overall validity holding (which was also 3:2 in a complex way) with a different fraction. The key UPSC-testable fact is that this was a 3:2 divided bench decision — not unanimous.
solution.final_explanation:
The Kihoto Hollohan judgment (1992) is notable both for its holdings and for the divided nature of the Constitution Bench.

• Option (a) — 5:3 majority: Incorrect. A five-judge Constitution Bench cannot produce a 5:3 split — the maximum minority on such a bench is 2. This option is mathematically impossible for a five-judge bench.
• Option (b) — Unanimous: Incorrect. The bench was sharply divided — the judgment was not unanimous.
• Option (c) — 4:1 majority: Incorrect. The finality clause was not struck down by a 4:1 majority.
• Option (d) — 3:2 majority: Correct. The Supreme Court's five-judge Constitution Bench was divided 3:2, with the majority striking down Paragraph 6(2) on the ground that excluding judicial review violated the basic structure of the Constitution (specifically, the rule of law and the principle of judicial oversight).

Value Addition:
• The basic structure doctrine — established in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) — was invoked to strike down the finality clause even though the 10th Schedule itself was upheld.
• The two dissenting judges believed the Speaker's decisions should be accorded greater finality and deference.
• Kihoto Hollohan also clarified that courts can intervene only after the Speaker's final order — not during the proceedings.

solution.concept_anchor: Structural lacunae in 10th Schedule — genuine vs fabricated
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) about the Speaker facing a conflict of interest is a real and widely cited lacuna — students who know this is a genuine problem may be drawn to it as the 'odd one out' thinking it is too obvious.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: Three options should describe genuine structural lacunae of the 10th Schedule; one should be a non-lacuna or fabricated concern.
Verify option (a): No time limit for Speaker's decision — genuine lacuna, widely acknowledged.
Verify option (b): Speaker has a conflict of interest when deciding cases involving their own party — genuine lacuna, highlighted in Nabam Rebia and academic literature.

Verify option (c): The Schedule's merger provision requires political party-level merger — this is a defined requirement in the law, not a lacuna. However, the argument can be made that it creates ambiguity.

Evaluate option (d): 'The 10th Schedule does not apply to members who vote against constitutional amendments' — this is fabricated. The Schedule applies to all party-directed votes including those on constitutional amendments. This is not a lacuna — it is a false statement about a non-existent exemption.
Option (d) is the odd one out — it describes a non-existent provision, not a real lacuna.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Options (a), (b), and (c) describe genuine structural problems identified by scholars, courts, and committees. Option (d) fabricates an exemption that does not exist — the anti-defection law applies to votes on constitutional amendments just as it does to any other party-directed vote. A student who focuses on 'which lacuna is most minor' rather than 'which is not a real lacuna' will miss the odd one out.
solution.final_explanation:
The 10th Schedule is widely critiqued for several structural gaps — but not every claimed gap is real.

• Option (a) — Real lacuna: The Schedule prescribes no time limit for the Speaker to decide a disqualification petition. Speakers have exploited this to delay decisions until the term of the legislature expires.
• Option (b) — Real lacuna: When the Speaker is a member of a faction whose opponents have filed the disqualification petition, the Speaker faces an inherent conflict of interest. The Schedule is silent on who decides in such cases — courts have had to step in (Nabam Rebia, 2016).
• Option (c) — Real legal question: The requirement that a merger occur at the political party level (not just within the legislature party) creates genuine interpretive difficulty in distinguishing a real merger from an engineered one — this is a genuine area of legal ambiguity.
• Option (d) — Not a real lacuna / fabricated: The 10th Schedule contains no exemption for votes on constitutional amendments. A party direction to vote for or against a constitutional amendment, if defied without prior permission, attracts disqualification just like any other vote. This option fabricates a non-existent provision.

Value Addition:
• The absence of a time limit is considered the most exploited structural gap in the 10th Schedule.
• Scholars have also identified the absence of any independent adjudicatory body as a systemic problem.
• The Law Commission (170th Report) recommended the Election Commission as an alternative adjudicatory authority precisely to address the conflict of interest problem.

statement_analysis.statement: Pair 1 — 52nd Constitutional Amendment (1985): Inserted the 10th Schedule into the Constitution of India.

statement_analysis.statement: Pair 2 — Paragraph 2(1)(a): Disqualifies a member who formally resigns from the political party.
statement_analysis.reason: Paragraph 2(1)(a) covers 'voluntarily giving up membership,' which is broader than formal resignation — conduct implying severance of party ties is sufficient (Ravi Naik case). The pair understates the scope by saying 'formally resigns.'

statement_analysis.statement: Pair 3 — Paragraph 4 (Merger): Requires at least two-thirds of the legislature party to agree to the merger.
statement_analysis.reason: The two-thirds threshold for a valid merger under Paragraph 4 is correctly stated — this provision remains in force after the 91st Amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: Pair 4 — Speaker's decision under Paragraph 6: Is subject to judicial review only before the final order is passed.
statement_analysis.reason: Kihoto Hollohan held the opposite — judicial review is permissible only AFTER the final order, not before (not at the interlocutory stage). This pair reverses the rule.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) suggests three correct pairs, which tempts students who correctly identify Pairs 1 and 3 but are uncertain about Pair 2's 'formal resignation' nuance and may let it pass.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Pair 1: 52nd Amendment inserted the 10th Schedule — correct.

Evaluate Pair 3: Two-thirds threshold for merger — correct.

Only two pairs (1 and 3) are correct → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Pair 2 uses 'formally resigns' — which is a partial truth. Formal resignation is one way of giving up membership, but the law and judicial interpretation extend this to any conduct implying severance of party ties. Pair 4 reverses the Kihoto Hollohan rule: the holding was that courts can review only after the final order — not before. Students who know 'courts can review the Speaker's decision' may miss the critical timing element.

Only Pairs 1 and 3 are correctly stated.

solution.concept_anchor: Whip — conduit of political party direction, not the party itself
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is the strong distractor because 'whip' and 'political party direction' are so closely associated in common usage that students may treat them as identical — selecting the option that says the whip's instruction is itself the party direction.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The direction under Paragraph 2(1)(b) must be that of the 'political party' — the whip is the conduit, not the principal. The direction must originate from the authorised party body.
Eliminate option (b): The legislature party and political party are distinct — a direction from the legislature party's leader alone may not constitute a 'political party direction' in all cases.
Eliminate option (d): There is no requirement that every direction be issued in writing — the law does not specify the form of the direction.

Confirm option (c): The whip acts as the formal channel through which the political party communicates its direction to members inside the legislature — but the authority behind the direction is the political party, not the whip personally.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap operates between the whip (an instrument and office) and the political party (the principal authority). Students assume the whip's instruction is itself the party direction — but the 10th Schedule's language refers to the 'direction of the political party.' If a whip issues a direction without party authorisation, it may not constitute a valid direction under the Schedule. This has been litigated in several state-level cases.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between the whip and the anti-defection law is more nuanced than popular understanding suggests.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: While the whip communicates the party's direction, the direction must originate from the authorised body of the political party. The whip acts as the transmission mechanism — the authority lies with the political party organisation, not the whip as an individual.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The 'legislature party' and 'political party' are distinct entities. A direction from the legislature party leader may or may not constitute a direction from the 'political party' depending on the party's internal constitution and the authorisation given to that leader.
• Option (c) — Correct: The whip functions as the formal conduit through which the political party communicates its directions to members within the legislature. The disqualification under Paragraph 2(1)(b) is triggered when a member defies the political party's direction — the whip's role is to convey this direction.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The 10th Schedule does not specify that directions must be in writing — the form of communication is not prescribed.

Value Addition:
• The distinction between 'political party' and 'legislature party' became critically important in the Shiv Sena (2023) crisis.
• A whip's direction that exceeds the authorisation given by the political party may not constitute a valid direction under Paragraph 2(1)(b).
• The whip system in India has roots in Westminster practice but operates under constitutionally stricter conditions due to the anti-defection law.

solution.concept_anchor: Nabam Rebia — scope of Speaker's restraint and nemo judex principle

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court in Nabam Rebia vs Deputy Speaker held that a Speaker cannot decide any matter connected with the legislature once a notice for their removal is received by the House.
statement_analysis.reason: The ruling was specifically about disqualification petitions under the 10th Schedule — the Court did not hold that the Speaker is completely incapacitated on all matters once a removal notice is received. The restriction was targeted at the conflict of interest in disqualification proceedings.

statement_analysis.statement: The principle underlying the Nabam Rebia ruling is that no person should be a judge in their own cause — a maxim of natural justice applicable even to constitutional offices.
statement_analysis.reason: The Latin maxim nemo judex in causa sua was explicitly invoked by the Supreme Court as the foundation for restraining the Speaker from deciding disqualification petitions when the Speaker's own removal was pending.

statement_analysis.statement: Nabam Rebia (2016) arose in the context of a political crisis in the state of Arunachal Pradesh.
statement_analysis.reason: The case was a direct outcome of the Arunachal Pradesh political crisis of 2016, involving a challenge to the Speaker's actions during a period of severe political instability in the state.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) would include Statement 1 as correct, which is tempting for students who know the Speaker was restrained but overstate the scope of the restraint to 'all legislative functions.'
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: 'Any matter connected with the legislature' is an overstatement — the Nabam Rebia ruling restrained the Speaker specifically from deciding disqualification petitions during the pendency of a removal notice. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Nemo judex in causa sua was the explicit basis — Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Arunachal Pradesh political crisis — confirmed factually. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 employs a scope-extension — 'any matter connected with the legislature' is far broader than what Nabam Rebia actually held. The Court specifically targeted the conflict of interest in disqualification proceedings, not the Speaker's general legislative functions. Students who recall 'the Speaker was stopped by the Supreme Court' may not recall the precise scope of the restraint and accept Statement 1 as true.
solution.final_explanation:
Nabam Rebia vs Deputy Speaker (2016) is a landmark case on the boundaries of the Speaker's power under the 10th Schedule.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Nabam Rebia ruling did not incapacitate the Speaker on all matters. The specific holding was that the Speaker cannot proceed to decide disqualification petitions under the 10th Schedule when a notice for their own removal is pending. Expanding this to 'any matter connected with the legislature' is an overstatement not supported by the judgment.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Court explicitly applied the principle of nemo judex in causa sua — no one can be a judge in their own cause. The Speaker, facing a removal notice, had a personal interest in the outcome of the disqualification proceedings (since disqualifying members of the opposing faction would help the Speaker's faction maintain numbers). Natural justice required recusal.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The case emerged from the dramatic Arunachal Pradesh political crisis of 2016, in which the then-Governor's actions and the Speaker's disqualification orders were both challenged.

Value Addition:
• The Nabam Rebia judgment has been referred to a larger Constitution Bench for reconsideration — its precedential status is currently under review.
• Arunachal Pradesh political crisis also involved questions about the Governor's discretionary power to advance the assembly session.
• The case is relevant at the intersection of three constitutional provisions: the 10th Schedule, Article 179 (removal of Speaker), and Article 212 (non-justiciability of legislative proceedings).
